title: Temperature control and food safety records
siteNotes: The venue's own fridge and freezer limits, if stricter than the legal 8C (for example a 5C target)
The venue's own cooking and reheating target temperature, if it uses a higher figure than the FSA minimum
Where the daily temperature records and the Safer Food Better Business diary are kept, and who signs them off
Where the probe thermometers and probe wipes are kept, and how often the venue calibrates them
Who to tell when a fridge, freezer or hot-holding unit is out of temperature, and the venue's rule for what happens to the food
The venue's cooling method (blast chiller, ice bath or shallow trays) and where cooled food is labelled and stored
How the venue handles hot display or hot service for weddings and events
legalNotes: HACCP-based procedures and records: Regulation (EC) 852/2004 art. 5, as it applies in England. FSA Safer Food, Better Business (SFBB) is the FSA's way for smaller businesses to meet this. https://www.food.gov.uk/business-guidance/sfbb

Chilled food at 8C or below is a legal limit in England (Food Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013 Sch. 4). 5C or below is the FSA recommended target, not a legal limit. Verified against secondary sources; the FSA page could not be fetched.
Hot holding at 63C or above: legal requirement in England. Hot food may be held below 63C for up to two hours, once, if it is then used, or else chilled or thrown away. Verified in outline.

Cooking: FSA guidance for England is a core temperature of 70C for 2 minutes, or an equivalent combination: 60C for 45 minutes, 65C for 10 minutes, 75C for 30 seconds, 80C for 6 seconds. NOTE: the commonly quoted '75C for 2 minutes' is not the FSA figure; many kitchens use a higher target as their own policy, and that goes in siteNotes. Verified against secondary sources.
Cooling: FSA guidance is to cool food as quickly as possible, ideally within 90 minutes, to 8C or below. Not verified from the FSA page directly; treat 90 minutes as guidance, not law.

Reheating: reheat until steaming hot all the way through, and only once. The FSA numerical figure was not verified, so the session gives no number for reheating; the venue may set its own target (siteNotes).
Probe calibration: checking against iced water (0C) and boiling water (100C) is common good practice and is not a legal requirement. Not verified against the FSA page; flagged as good practice.
Not verified: freezer limits. None given in the session.

Review 6 Oct 2026: re-checked against GOV.UK/FSA 'Cooking food safely' and chilling guidance (via search summaries). Confirmed: core cooking 70C for 2 minutes with equivalents 60C/45 min, 65C/10 min, 75C/30 s, 80C/6 s; hot food kept at or above 63C, with up to 2 hours below 63C permitted once before it must be cooled to 8C or below or thrown away; cool as fast as possible, ideally within 90 minutes; reheat until steaming hot throughout, once only. No wording changed. The gravy check (55C, reheat to 63C or above) is acceptable because the food has not been cooled and reheated before; the venue may prefer 'steaming hot all through' as its own reheating rule (siteNotes).

cards.title: Temperature control and food safety records
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- state the key safe temperatures
- use and clean a probe correctly
- keep the records and act when something is out of range

cards.title: Know the numbers
cards.body: Bacteria multiply in the gap between cold storage and hot holding. We keep food cold, cook it through, and keep it hot. Your manager will show you any stricter limits the venue uses.

items.label: Fridge: the legal maximum for chilled food
The recommended target, to stay safely below
Core cooking for 2 minutes, or an equivalent

cards.title: Cook it right through
cards.body: The centre of the food must be hot enough for long enough. The FSA standard is 70°C for 2 minutes at the core. Other equivalent combinations work too, such as 75°C for 30 seconds or 80°C for 6 seconds. Your manager will show you the venue's own target.

visual.caption: Core temperature and the time it must be held (not to scale)

cards.title: Hot, then cooled fast
cards.body: Hot food on the pass, a bain-marie or at a wedding buffet must stay at **63°C or above**. If food has to cool, get it cold quickly, ideally within 90 minutes, then into the fridge. Reheat only once, and until steaming hot all the way through. Your manager will show you the cooling method here.

items.title: Cool fast
items.text: Small shallow portions, off the heat

cards.title: Using the probe
cards.body: A probe only helps if it is clean and accurate. Put the tip in the centre or thickest part of the food. Clean it between foods, especially from raw to cooked. Calibrate it regularly, for example in iced water, which should read about 0°C. Your manager will show you where the probes and wipes are and when to calibrate.

cards.title: If it is not written down
cards.body: Daily records prove that we did the checks. Write the reading when you take it, not later from memory, and sign it. Your manager will show you where the records are kept and who checks them.

cards.title: Out of temperature
cards.body: Do not hide it and do not guess. If a fridge reads above 8°C, hot food is below 63°C, or food has not reached its cooking temperature, act at once.

items.title: Fix it
items.text: Keep cooking, reheat or move the food

items.title: Tell your manager
items.text: Before you use or throw away the food

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Chilled food: 8°C or below by law. Aim for 5°C.
- Hot food held at 63°C or above.
- Core cooking: 70°C for 2 minutes, or an equivalent.
- Probe the centre, clean it between foods, and keep it calibrated.
- Write records at the time. If a reading is wrong, tell your manager.

cards.q: The walk-in fridge reads 11°C when you arrive. What do you do first?
options: Note it and check again at the end of the shift
Turn the dial down and carry on
Record it and tell your manager before using the food
Throw everything away without telling anyone
cards.why: A fridge above 8°C is out of limit. It must be recorded and reported so the food can be judged safely.

cards.q: Hot food on the pass should be held at 63°C or above.
cards.why: 63°C or above stops bacteria multiplying. Below that it is on the clock.

cards.q: Where do you put the probe in a chicken breast to check it is cooked?
options: Against the pan
In the thickest part, the centre
In the thin tip at the edge
Just under the skin
cards.why: The centre of the thickest part is the coldest spot, so that is where it must reach temperature.

cards.q: Which TWO are correct core cooking checks for England?
options: 70°C held for 2 minutes
50°C held for 5 minutes
80°C held for 6 seconds
60°C held for 2 minutes
40°C held for 30 minutes
cards.why: 70°C for 2 minutes and 80°C for 6 seconds are both on the FSA's list of equivalent combinations.

cards.q: You probe raw burgers, then want to check cooked ones. What first?
options: Nothing, the heat will kill any germs
Wipe it with a dry cloth
Rinse it under the tap
Clean and sanitise the probe
cards.why: A dirty probe can carry bacteria from raw food to cooked food. Clean it between every use.

cards.q: Which temperature is the recommended target for chilled food, rather than the legal limit?
cards.why: The legal maximum is 8°C. The FSA recommends aiming for 5°C or below to stay safely under it.

cards.q: Leaving a deep pot of hot soup on the bench is a good way to cool it quickly.
cards.why: A deep pot cools slowly. Divide food into small shallow portions so it cools fast, then label and chill it.

cards.q: A buffet tray of gravy has been reading 55°C for ten minutes. What do you do?
options: Leave it, it is still warm to the touch
Stir it and look again at the end of service
Top it up with fresh gravy from the pan
Heat it back to 63°C or above
cards.why: Hot food must be held at 63°C or above. Below that, bacteria can multiply, so act and tell your manager.

cards.q: Why do we write the fridge reading down at the time we take it?
options: It makes the fridge run a little colder
It proves the check really happened
It means tomorrow's check can be skipped
It counts as the weekly cleaning record
cards.why: Records are the proof the check was done. Writing them at the time keeps them honest.

cards.q: Which TWO are right for looking after a probe?
options: Check it reads about 0°C in iced water
Wipe it on your apron between foods
Clean and sanitise it between raw and cooked
Leave it in the pan to stay warm
Check it only when it breaks
cards.why: Calibrate regularly and clean between foods, especially raw to cooked, so the probe never spreads bacteria.
